articles.description:
Every so often I suffer from what I call "Emacs Fatigue". It's closely related to "Text File Fatigue". Using Emacs tends to pull one toward using it for everything, which is what I'd done. Then, I simply grow tired of staring at the same thing every day. When this happens, I "decide" to uproot my life and move my notes into something else. This time, that something else was Bear.
Bear is great. It's solid, beautiful, and refreshingly simple. It syncs flawlessly (for free) and runs on macOS and iOS. It's also inexpensive. It uses an SQLite database, which doesn't bother me. Databases are great at this stuff. All the "But but what if the database...?!" talk is mostly hearsay anyway.
The thing that made me twitchy was that it felt like my notes were "in there". It's not the database. It's the fact that everything is in an app, and that app makes me need to use that app. This is how I'd started to feel about Emacs, but mostly due to Org mode.
Bear is macOS and iOS only, which should be fine for someone like me who has "decided" to live on macOS. And yet, Linux continues to emit a low-grade hum in the back of my head that I can't ignore.
If I don't want my notes in Org mode files, but I'm still drawn toward Emacs, what should I do? Denote! That's where they'd all started in the first place, but as .org not .md. I'd nearly forgotten that Denote handles Markdown files natively. One Emacs configuration change and I was back where I belong. And since Bear notes are already Markdown, all it took was an export and a (Claude Code-assisted) conversion script for file names, links, and attachments.
So yes, I've done that thing where I quit using Emacs only to come crawling back later. I know better, but knowing better doesn't stop me. Maybe I'll work on a sync/bridge between Denote and Bear. That would be neat.

I was on my Mac this morning, just minding my own business, when suddenly I found myself using the Linux laptop, and I liked it.
On Sunday mornings, I do system maintenance. This means running updates on all my computers. Right now, that's five machines: one Linux desktop, two Linux laptops, one Mac desktop, and one Mac laptop. Yes, that's too many, but it is what it is.
Both Linux laptops run CachyOS, which is Arch-based, so there are always updates.
I started with the Framework. Once it was updated and rebooted, I pulled the latest tweaks to my Emacs config, to make sure it worked on Linux. I've been leaning toward using macOS exclusively, so I haven't been testing things on Linux as much. Everything worked, though.
While typing on the Framework, the first thing I thought about was how much I prefer typing on it to typing on the MacBook Air. Then I remembered how much I like the idea of Linux. Then I noticed that Emacs starts up more than twice as fast on the Framework for some reason. Then I remembered that the best (and only) way to have consistent Emacs key bindings on Linux is to, well, use Emacs.
All this to say that the conflict between running macOS, Linux, or both is still a thing. As troublesome and complex as it can be, I think the answer will always be "both". Surely I can manage it, right? Maybe if I only use the laptops for simple things like blogging, browsing, or journaling, things will be easy enough. I'll never be able to settle on one or the other. Just admit it.
I'm on the couch typing this in Emacs using the Framework, both things I told myself a week ago that I'd stop doing. My stupid brain is always mucking things up.

quick post on Sacha’s solution to a problem posed by David Pape. I thought it was a nice solution but then 0-_-0_ pointed out that abo-abo had already solved this problem with his tiny library. So I wrote about that and prepared to move on.


I was not allowed to. Frequent commenter Phil remarked in my original post that he would use a keyboard macro. He suggested that that would make sense for those of us who who seldom need to enter a sequence of ranges like Pape. In Pape’s case this was something that he needed to do a lot so a solution like Sacha’s or abo-abo’s make sense. I agree with Phil. A keyboard macro is exactly how I would solve this problem given that I seldom have it.


This seems pretty obvious and might not be worth writing about except that Phil’s solution showed me something that I didn’t know: You can set the initial value of the counter with a Ctrl+u n where n is the desired initial value. That’s a lot easier than using Ctrl+x Ctrl+k Ctrl+c to do the job.


As a final note, I think that Phil had a typo in his macro. As far as I can tell it should be

C-u 47 <f3> # <f3> , SPC <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4>


At least that’s what works for me.


It turns out that I regularly use a macro with a counter so I’m really happy to learn that the counter can be set so easily.

articles.description:
org-use-speed-commands all the time when navigating and performing actions on org headlines, but I think I have found a friction point, something that just feels a little off.



When the point is on * and then you press the key t, it calls org-todo via org-self-insert-command. Fast, but the feel is off, the point stays on the stars, so I have to move right before I can type the headline.









The reason is in org-todo itself. It has a cursor fixup that parks point just after the keyword, but only when point is not at beginning of line. Speed keys by definition run at beginning of line (org-speed-command-activate requires (bolp)), so the fixup never fires for exactly the keys that would benefit most.



There is no custom option for it, so I added a small :after advice:



(defun my/org-todo-stop-after-keyword (&rest _)
  "Move point to just after TODO keyword when `org-todo' leaves it at BOL.
Speed command `t' (via `org-self-insert-command') runs with point at
beginning of headline, where `org-todo' skips its cursor fixup."
  (when (and (bolp) (org-at-heading-p))
    (when (looking-at org-todo-line-regexp)
      (goto-char (or (match-end 2) (match-end 1)))
      (when (looking-at " ") (forward-char 1)))))
(advice-add 'org-todo :after #'my/org-todo-stop-after-keyword)

* Test with point on * plus t becomes * TODO Test with point on Test, ready to type. Same for cycling * TODO to * DONE.



Small change, but speed keys finally feel like they finish the job instead of leaving me parked on the margin!

Will voice kill the keyboard. No. Will the way we interact with Emacs, and computers in general, change drastically? No.
Star Trek has a mythical AI/computer that responds to voice commands and interacts with you to clarify or note other work that may pertain to what you wanted. Evidently the interface is so ubiquitous that Scotty talks to a mouse noting it's "quaint" to need to push it and type on a keyboard to interact with a computer.
But if we watch the bridge of any Star Trek show people aren't talking the whole time. They're tapping screens to get the computer to do things for them. Theoretically the captain could tell the ship where he wants to go and let the computer do it, but he issues a command and then someone types in the needed commands to the ship so it goes in the expected direction.
I work at home in a solo office space. I could talk to my computer and it would disturb no one, except me. I'd be unable to listen to music on my stereo at the same time just in case the computer couldn't understand my words versus the song.
I don't think keyboards are going anywhere any time soon. They provide an unambiguous interface to your computer that doesn't disturb others. I think that those loving Emacs interactions like they use it will continue to do so as they do now because it's the most efficient way to control the Emacs interface.

extolling the power of plain text. It’s a notion that’s familiar to all us Emacs users and even more so to Org users. We Org users (or more generally Markdown and other markup users) can write plain text and have it formatted for output in a variety of ways. The point is, the text stays text and is readable even without the formatting.


As nickb says, text written today will still be readable 50 years from now. Sure, UTF-8 and the other Unicode formats can and do add new characters from time to time but text written today will have the same meaning even if new characters are added.


The most important aspect is that you’ll own your data no matter what programs come and go. Emacs isn’t going anywhere but even if it did, it wouldn’t matter. Text will still be readable and something like Org or Markdown will still make intended formatting obvious even if Org and Markdown no longer exist.


Nickb acknowledges that text is not the right answer for everything. You wouldn’t, for example, want to represent a photograph in plain text and there are lots of other examples. Still, for many applications, plain text is not only sufficient but probably the better solution.

articles.description:
David Pape asked:




I just typed



>Closes: #47, #48, #49, #50, #51, #52, #53, #54



into a commit description, all by hand.



Is there a way in Emacs to expand some kind of range description to make this easier? 😅



I want to expand strings like "5-10, 15-18, 3" into numbers.




Hmm, could be useful. It reminds me of how page ranges work, which will be handy if I want to tinker with PDFs. Let's see if something like this works:




(defun sacha-parse-page-range (s)
  "Parse a page range string and return a list of numbers.
Ex: 1-5
2-4, 6-10
1 4 7-9
3-11/2   - this one specifies an increment"
  (seq-mapcat
   (lambda (part)
     (let ((nums (mapcar 'string-to-number (split-string part " *[-/] *"))))
       (if (= (length nums) 1)
           nums
         (number-sequence (elt nums 0) (elt nums 1) (elt nums 2)))))
   (split-string s "[, \t\n\r]+")))

(ert-deftest sacha-parse-page-range ()
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "5-10")
                 '(5 6 7 8 9 10)))
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "1-5, 8")
                 '(1 2 3 4 5 8)))
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "1 4 7-9")
                 '(1 4 7 8 9)))
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "3-11/2")
                 '(3 5 7 9 11))))

(defun sacha-issue-range (range)
  "Expand RANGE to a list of issues and insert them."
  (interactive "MRange (ex: 1-5, 7): ")
  (let ((s (mapconcat (lambda (n) (format "#%d" n))
                      (sacha-parse-page-range range)
                      ", ")))
    (when (called-interactively-p 'any)
      (insert s))
    s))

articles.description:
What’s the future of Emacs? He asks that question in the context of assuming that Emacs will continue to exist for any timeline that matters to us. But how, he asks, will we use it?


The answer that will occur to most of us is speech mediated input á la Star Trek TNG. We’ll simply tell Emacs what we want it to do and it will do it. But think about that for a moment. Would you really want to dictate the code for your latest program to the computer? Or would you even want to dictate your documentation, story, or letter to your computer?


Sure, you could say something like, “Computer write a program to do such and such.” but then you’re not using Emacs at all. The same for asking the computer to write something for you. That—more or less—is here today but most of us don’t like the results and, again, we’re not really using Emacs in those situations.


For my part, my written thoughts are always much better organized than my spoken ones so even with  capable voice input, I’d much prefer to use the keyboard. Maiorana agrees. He points back to a couple of episodes from Tales From the Darkside1 in which people use the keyboard to do magic with the computer. For him, Meta+x is the spell that enables the magic and he’s very attached to it. Like me, he doesn’t anticipate abandoning the keyboard.


What do you think? Will we still use the keyboard or will we move on to something better?

Earlier this year I added Ghostel to my
Emacs configuration. Ghostel is a terminal emulator for Emacs that uses
Ghostty's engine underneath. It is a delight to use
especially with the TUI applications.
Nested Emacs frame problem
I use Emacs in daemon
mode,
and then use emacsclient to open new frames from the daemon. To use the same
Emacs daemon when opening files through other programs such as git, sops, I have
a small shell script ee configured as my default EDITOR. It opens a new
Emacs frame in the terminal.
#!/bin/sh

exec emacsclient --create-frame --no-window-system "$@"

When I run this script from Ghostel, it opens a nested Emacs frame in Ghostel's
terminal session.

Solution
Emacs sets an environment variable INSIDE_EMACS for shells and subprocesses.
The script use this variable to check if it is launched from Ghostel and use the
--reuse-frame flag to open the new buffer in the current frame.
#!/bin/sh

if [ "$INSIDE_EMACS" = "ghostel" ]
then
  exec emacsclient --reuse-frame "$@"
fi

exec emacsclient --create-frame --no-window-system "$@"
articles.title: Ankit Gadiya: Fix nested Emacs frames

The relationship between sports and the place where those games are played is largely a matter of fans developing a strong but mostly manageable addiction to their own pheromones. Ritual and iconography matter more than the actual results when the results don't meet the need; the first two are stable and reliable in a way the third will never be. It has always been thus.
And so Mike Ditka, whose death at age 86 was announced by his family Friday morning, was and remains still Chicago in ways that no other figure in any other city could manage. Ditka explained Chicago's view of itself from head to toe, vocal inflections to hand gestures, minor local biases to general worldview. Chicago is Ditka just as Ditka was Chicago, and that self-reverential truth will remain true even after he's gone.
Ditka was quite literally the face of the Bears from the moment he left the University of Pittsburgh to seek his fortune in football 65 years ago. His helmet with the white single-bar facemask and his gashed-up face behind it was the image of choice in their 1963 championship, the one that interrupted the Decade of Lombardi. Ditka's contractual intransigence in the face of the team's iconic (and iconically vice-gripped) owner, George Halas, reinforced that status despite the six-year endgame in Philadelphia and then Dallas that completed his playing career. Even Ditka's Super Bowl championship with Dallas in 1971 felt a bit odd, in that Why is that Chicago guy celebrating next to Roger Staubach? kind of way. He sent himself into exile rather than take what Halas was offering, but Ditka never really left.

Geriatric Jonathan has made the news again, this time for having his genome sequenced. The Aldabra giant tortoise, who is estimated to be 194 years old, is the oldest known land animal on the planet. (The ocean, which teems with glass sponges thousands of years old and Greenland sharks that have been swimming for centuries, takes longevity to different extremes.) As such, it is understandable why scientists would want to sequence Jonathan's genome. He's lived a long freaking time.
Yet many of the headlines heralding this new inquiry into Jonathan's venerable age, which was published in Science Advances, have made me laugh with their implications that we may follow in Jonathan's closely spaced footsteps. Consider Reuters: "A 194-year-old tortoise, world's oldest land animal, may hold clues to longer life." Or take The Times: "Has 194-year-old tortoise Jonathan taught us the secret to longer life?" What are the clues and secrets to Jonathan's extremely long life? Mainly there is one: Jonathan is a turtle.
I can hardly blame these publications for this headline format; the blueprint was in the press releases issued by the University of Cambridge and Vanderbilt University, both of which framed Jonathan as potentially holding the secret to a long and healthy life, which he very well could! The headline in IFLScience—"We Finally Know How Jonathan The Tortoise, The World's Oldest Land Animal, Is Still Alive And Kicking At 194"—is easily answered the same way. Jonathan the tortoise is alive and kicking because he had the good luck to be born an Aldabra giant tortoise. Were Jonathan a human guy, he would not be alive.

Having leisurely picked it up one day without expecting to be taken in, Jon Krakauer’s Into Thin Air arrested me from the first page. “Among my five teammates who reached the top [of Mount Everest], four … perished in a rogue storm,” Krakauer writes. “By the time I’d descended to Base Camp nine climbers from four expeditions were dead, and three more lives would be lost before the month was out.” Twelve deaths seemed to me a Shakespearean number. But the more I read about mountaineering, the more I realized that there was nothing extraordinary, per se, about tragedy in the mountains. On Everest alone, as many as 10 people die on average every year, a number that keeps climbing as temperatures rise. Krakauer’s book is so affecting because he refuses to look at this fact with nonchalance.
In that, Krakauer seems to be a bit of an outlier. Nonchalance is a common trait in adventurers whose impossible feats break through to the mainstream; consider Alex Honnold’s maddeningly blasé attitude toward his own chances in Free Solo. For those of us who are fearful, this ability to repress or at least temper the fear of death is the root of our fascination with extreme sports athletes. Most depictions of their exploits ask an obvious question: Why do this? But that’s a deceiving question, because the answer, at least as far as the psychologies on display are concerned, is equally obvious: Why not? When he was asked why he wanted to climb Mount Everest, George Mallory—the English mountaineer who was among the first to break trail on Everest, and who died on his third attempt to summit the mountain in 1924—famously replied: “Because it is there.” But the rest of his quote is just as telling a glimpse into the reasoning of the high-elevation climber. The urge, he said, is “a part, I suppose, of man’s desire to conquer the universe.”

If one wanted to understand the alarming state of international politics in the Western Hemisphere through a single story, it'd be hard to beat Jose Antonio Kast visiting CECOT this past January.
Kast spent nearly 20 years at the extreme right fringe of Chilean politics, mostly crusading against women's rights. His father was a Nazi, and not in any sort of metaphorical sense: He served as an Oberleutnant in the Wehrmacht in World War II. Various members of the Kast family also worked for the Pinochet dictatorship and have dedicated their lives to revanche. Last December, Kast won Chile's presidential election thanks in part to Donald Trump throwing his weight around, and before he took office, he went up to El Salvador to visit its notorious CECOT prison. Kast said he was interested in how to "import good ideas and proposals," such as the mass torture compound, in his quest to militarize Chile against the specter of narcoterrorists and illegal immigrants, and in doing so bring it into close collaboration with the Trump administration.
This sort of thing has been happening all across Latin America since Trump strode back into power, with a rapidly dwindling handful of notable exceptions. The two most-populated countries cling to leftist rule, for now anyway. Claudia Sheinbaum's government is quite popular in Mexico and has managed to keep the U.S. relatively at bay, while Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is still in charge of Brazil. However, Lula underperformed in the first round of Brazilian elections this past Sunday, and Brazil is on the verge of electing Flavio Bolsonaro. The eldest son of the currently jailed and constantly leaking fascist former president assuming office of the second-most populous country in the Western Hemisphere would represent a total victory for the Trump-aligned right-wing movement in South America, and would by extension be a disaster for the country, the hemisphere, and the planet. How did we get here, and what tensions animate this broad coalition?
